https://www.politico.eu/article/germany-.text: German commentators are calling it a modern-day “ miracle .” Hundreds of thousands of worshippers are walking away from their churches each year. The money, however, keeps rolling in. Some 660,000 people formally quit the country’s Catholic and Protestant churches in 2025, freeing them from a levy automatically charged to registered members as a percentage of their income tax bill. Despite the exodus, the two institutions collected more than €12.5 billion through the church tax for the 2025 fiscal year, up from around €12.4 billion in 2024. The apparent miracle has a decidedly earthly explanation: Rising wages and Germany’s progressive tax system mean the shrinking pool of members is paying more. “At first glance, the development may seem contradictory,” a spokesperson for the Evangelical Church in Germany — the umbrella organization representing Germany’s regional Protestant churches — said. “The reason is that church tax is calculated based on individual income tax.” Advertisement Members of Germany’s Catholic and Protestant churches and some Jewish communities pay an additional religious tax equal to 8 or 9 percent of their income tax liability, even if they don’t attend services. In 2021, the most recent year for which comprehensive data is available, more than 29 million people paid church tax in Germany, amounting to almost half of all income taxpayers in Europe’s largest economy. The German Finance Ministry’s 2025 payroll tax tables suggests that a single employee without children earning €50,000 gross a year pays approximately €600 in church tax annually on top of income tax, depending on the federal state. Someone earning €70,000 per year pays more than €1,000. People are registered as part of their religious community at birth or at local government offices. To stop paying the church tax, they must formally leave through a process known as Kirchenaustritt , or “church exit.” The procedure varies across Germany’s federal states but typically requires appearing in person at a registry office or local court to submit a declaration. Most states also charge an administrative fee. While those who deregister can still attend services as a visitor and access some church services, they are not allowed to have a church wedding, be a godparent or be guaranteed a church burial. In 2025, some 310,000 left the Catholic Church, while around 350,000 left one of Germany’s regional Protestant churches. Church exit The reasons people give for formally leaving their religious communities range from feeling less connected to the church to simply wanting to save money. “People are leaving the Church because they feel it no longer plays a role in their lives,” said Matthias Kopp, director of communications for the German Bishops’ Conference. “Added to this are the scandals of recent years, which have called the Church’s credibility into question,” he added. “There are also people — though this is by no means the primary reason — who leave the Church because of the church tax.” “These are processes of alienation to which we must respond,” said Kopp. For Jana Keil, a 33-year-old accountant from Berlin, the decision was both financial and moral. “I no longer wanted to support the system with church tax in light of the [child sex] abuse scandals,” she said. Lukas Heinich, a 23-year-old working student, said he formally left after completing his apprenticeship because he “didn’t feel like paying the tax or supporting the church.” That church tax revenues continue to rise despite the exodus is down to the types of taxpayers choosing to remain church members. Those who are still paying church tax in Germany are “probably the higher earners,” said Zareh Asatryan, professor of empirical economics at the University of Münster. “Those that stay will naturally earn more income because of inflation plus real wage growth, and they will just generate more revenue.” A miracle with an end date? But the continued rise in church tax revenue masks significant long-term challenges — and raises questions about how long the trend can last. While those revenues are going up, they are “relatively sluggish” and “haven’t been increasing by a lot,” said Asatryan. The increase in revenue from the church tax is considerably lower than the increase in revenue from income tax. State revenue from wage and income taxes rose by 6.65 percent in 2025, said Kopp, whereas church tax revenue increased by 1.93 percent. “Long-term projections indicate that church tax revenue will decline significantly over the coming decades as church membership continues to decrease,” said the spokesperson for the Evangelical Church in Germany. Protestant churches are already preparing for their income to decrease “through long-term planning processes,” said the spokesperson. “Without this system, the church’s religious, social and charitable work would not be possible on its current scale.”

https://www.baltictimes.com/valainis_cal.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Valainis calls on government to prepare in timely manner possible support measures for high fuel prices 2026-07-28 LETA/TBT Staff RIGA - Economics Minister Viktors Valainis (Greens/Farmers) has sent a letter to the Cabinet of Ministers (MK) calling for timely preparations to be made for the possible implementation of support measures in response to fuel prices, the Ministry of Economics (EM) informed LETA. On Monday, July 27, Valainis sent a letter to the Cabinet of Ministers, informing the government that the situation in the fuel market is becoming increasingly volatile after having been relatively stable. The sharp rise in prices for crude oil and petroleum products on global markets has reignited an upward trend in fuel prices, while persistent high geopolitical uncertainty poses a risk of further price increases. In his letter, the minister calls on the government to begin preparatory work in a timely manner for the possible activation of support measures. This involves identifying existing and potential sources of funding, as well as preparing potential solutions. The ministry notes that from July 21 to July 27, the price of Brent crude oil rose by 14.5 percent, while the price of ICE Low Sulphur Gasoil rose by 17.1 percent. Valainis points out that none of the aforementioned price thresholds have been reached yet, but the rise in fuel prices this week clearly shows that the situation is becoming increasingly tense. In his view, it is necessary to take preventive action rather than wait until a crisis has already occurred. The previously adopted decision to extend the excise tax reduction on fuel is currently helping to mitigate the impact of rising prices. The minister notes that developing support measures under extraordinary circumstances requires significantly more time, while delayed action can create significant political, economic, and social pressure at a time when residents and businesses are already feeling the sharp rise in costs. The Ministry of Economics will continue to monitor fuel prices, track developments in energy markets, and, if necessary, propose specific decisions to the MK to ensure a timely and effective response to further increases in fuel prices. Following the July 21 government meeting, Valainis told LETA that the government has outlined possible scenarios for action in the event the situation were to worsen, and that the government had also discussed support measures to be implemented even under a moderate development scenario. Valainis noted that the rise in fuel prices has created additional costs in the public sector, including in the interior and health sectors. Therefore, the government will continue to monitor the situation and work to prevent any reduction in the availability of services provided to residents. Commenting on possible support mechanisms, the minister said that, if necessary, additional funding would be allocated from the state budget. As reported, a law on limiting the increase in fuel prices, which provides for short-term measures aimed at mitigating the impact of price hikes on the Latvian economy and population, came into force on April 1. The law provides for a temporary reduction in the excise duty on diesel fuel from the current EUR 467 to EUR 396 per 1,000 liters. For marked agricultural diesel, the excise duty rate is set at EUR 21 per 1,000 liters. The reduced rates are in effect from April 1 to the end of the year. https://movieweb.com/war-movies-most-dis.text: By Adam Symchuk Published Aug 2, 2026, 4:30 PM EDT Canadian-born reporter and editor Adam Symchuk has been writing on the topic of film, TV, and literature for over a decade. Starting with an emphasis on Asian film, literature and manga, his love of interntional cinema set the groundwork for decades of obsession with film. Sign in to your MovieWeb account Add Us Add on Google Preferred Source Google Discover Google News Summary Generate a summary of this story Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Thread 1 Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap Disturbing cinema has been a longtime focus of my relationship with the medium, from international films to dark comedies , and seeking these out has challenged my understanding of a lot of things in a way I have found genuinely rewarding. I know I am not unique in this. There is a vocal fandom that thrives on difficult content while still happily enjoying lighter fare, and approaching tough subjects is essential to what cinema is as an art form. One of the hardest subjects of all, though, is war and the various atrocities that come with it. To put this list together, I went back through my log of everything I have watched and pulled the titles I found most shocking. The reasons vary; sometimes the violence is what does the damage, and sometimes it is the sheer absence of humanity on display. There are plenty of disturbing war and war-adjacent films out there, but these ten are the ones that stuck. Why You Should Trust Me: I have been writing on film for over a decade, often with a focus on niche and international offerings. Here at MovieWeb, I have curated lists for disturbing, challenging cinema to help push recognition of overlooked titles. Honorable Mentions Five films had me going back and forth on whether to include them in the main list. I ultimately decided they were better placed here: Grave of the Fireflies (1988): The obvious omission, and only because I decided to keep the list live-action. Isao Takahata's animated account of two children starving to death in the last months of the Pacific War is utterly devastating, and still deserves the recommendation. The Ascent (1977): Larisa Shepitko's final feature is a Belarusian partisan story shot in a whiteout that grows more oppressive the longer you sit with the picture. The interrogation sequence at the center is one of the most quietly terrifying stretches you will find. Son of Saul (2015): László Nemes locks the camera to the back of a Sonderkommando prisoner's head and keeps the atrocity in soft focus at the edge of the frame. A phenomenal experiment that sends your eyes wandering to the corners out of morbid curiosity, and the approach makes the film niche but well worth a watch if the subject interests you. City of Life and Death (2009): Lu Chuan's black-and-white account of the Nanjing Massacre, told through several characters including a Japanese soldier and a child. The closing sequence, a victory ritual staged over the ruins, is one of the strangest and most disquieting endings in modern war cinema. Caterpillar (2010): Set during the Second Sino-Japanese War, a soldier who has lost his limbs and can no longer function is paraded home as a war hero. Once the glory fades and everyone moves on, his wife is left to care for him alone. Much like Johnny Got His Gun , Koji Wakamatsu's film turns anti-war sentiment into a deeply uncomfortable portrait of what a body brings back from the front. 'The Grey Zone' (2001) There Is No Exit Lions Gate Films IMDb: 7.0/10 | Letterboxd: 3.6/5 The Grey Zone dramatizes the Sonderkommando uprising at Auschwitz in October 1944. These were the Jewish prisoners forced to shepherd new arrivals into the gas chambers, empty them, and burn the bodies. Their story takes a turn when a teenage girl is found alive under a pile of corpses, and the men have to decide what to do with her while a rebellion is already in motion. The film flopped and drew mixed reviews, and I will admit a few of the choices did not land for me; casting familiar American actors like David Arquette, Steve Buscemi, and Harvey Keitel with no accents pulled me out of the story more than once. Where director Tim Blake Nelson thrives, though, is in building a scenario with absolutely no redemptive exit, which turns every conversation into men weighing their own morality against another hour of survival . Over time, The Grey Zone has built a deserved reputation as among the toughest American features of its decade. 'Red Angel' (1966) Addiction, Bodies, and the Void Daiei Film IMDb: 7.8/10 | Letterboxd: 3.9/5 Red Angel follows Nurse Sakura Nishi through the Japanese campaign in China in 1939, from a rear-line hospital to a forward surgical unit where amputation is essentially the only available treatment. Yasuzo Masumura, one of the godfathers of the Japanese New Wave , shoots the operating theater as an assembly line of unending suffering. Nishi's only reprieve is a relationship with a morphine-addicted surgeon. If you have never seen a Masumura movie, this one is a solid place to start. Much of his work lands in more disturbing territory, but always with a focus on character study and social commentary. Red Angel is among his most visually stunning pictures, and the introduction of eroticism adds a whole extra layer of desperation: no other war film I have seen conflates desire and dismemberment this calmly . The closing shot is tragic and iconic. This one is also more accessible than most of the list, with beauty and horror swirling around the screen at a dreamlike pace. 'Kanal' (1957) Doom Announced in the First Minute KADR IMDb: 7.9/10 | Letterboxd: 4.1/5 Kanal picks up a company of Polish Home Army fighters in the collapsing final days of the 1944 Warsaw Uprising, as they descend into the city's sewer system hoping to reach the city center. In the dark, unable to read any directions, the fighters find themselves trapped in a never-ending maze, fearful of the war above and the unknown in the murky below. Andrzej Wajda's film is a vastly underrated war picture that seldom gets the discussion it deserves. The story opens on a grim note, with a narrator telling you flatly that the men you are looking at are living their final hours. The first half plays out above ground and is punishing enough on its own, but the latter half traces desperate men and women through the sewers, stripped of whatever honor they thought they had, unable to reach the surface and slowly dying in the dark . Claustrophobic, horrific, tragic, and an often overlooked war classic. 'Men Behind the Sun' (1988) The Horrors of Unit 731 Grand Essex Enterprises IMDb: 6.1/10 | Letterboxd: 3.1/5 Men Behind the Sun dramatizes the operations of Unit 731, the Imperial Japanese Army's biological warfare division in occupied Manchuria. The story is nominally told through a group of teenage cadets assigned to the facility, but the overwhelming focus is on staging the tortures themselves. Real experiments are recreated here, including subjects taken through the stages of frostbite, pressure chamber deaths, and live vivisection. I was hesitant to include this one, because I do not consider Men Behind the Sun a "good" movie, but if the measure is disturbing, then leaving off this highly controversial title would be a serious omission . Does the film have any validity as artistic expression? Some, and mostly in how precisely it documents what was actually done. Director Mou Tun-Fei made this out of open anger at the Imperial Japanese Army, and that anger comes through in the rawest, most graphic way possible. Even so, I would advise most people to skip this one, since the production also used questionable methods to chase authenticity, and the results are stomach-churning. 'Threads' (1984) Nuclear War as a Government Report IMDb: 8.0/10 | Letterboxd: 4.2/5 Threads opens as a modest kitchen-sink drama about a young couple in Sheffield dealing with an unplanned pregnancy, before a NATO and Warsaw Pact escalation turns the film into something else entirely: a portrait of nuclear fallout. Director Mick Jackson and writer Barry Hines consulted scientists and civil defense planners at length to give an authentic account of such a disaster, working through the initial blast, the firestorm, radiation sickness, the collapse of medical infrastructure, nuclear winter, and then years forward into a barely literate agrarian remnant. This one hits hard, and it is wild to think the BBC broadcast the whole thing to the public, feeding straight into Cold War paranoia to instill a deeper sense of fear in viewers. Nothing before or since has modeled the end of a society with such chilling accuracy, and the closing freeze-frame is among the most despairing images ever put on television. As a made-for-TV movie , the budget was never going to be there, but the roughness works in the film's favor and makes the whole thing feel more authentic as ordinary citizens suffer through a nuclear nightmare and societal collapse. 'Fires on the Plain' (1959) Starvation Past the Last Taboo Daiei Film IMDb: 7.9/10 | Letterboxd: 4.1/5 Fires on the Plain drops Private Tamura into the disintegration of the Japanese army on Leyte in late 1944. Tubercular and turned away by both his unit and the field hospital, he is essentially directed to go off somewhere and die. Kon Ichikawa follows Tamura across the ravaged island, with the remains of the army wandering in feral groups and fighting off starvation. Eventually the survivors start passing around what they call "monkey meat," the euphemism they have settled on for cannibalism, and the last of their humanity goes with it. Director Kon Ichikawa took the great taboo subject of the Pacific War and filmed it without a single note of moralizing, making for one of the bleakest films ever to come out of a major Japanese studio. There are no redeeming stories here, just a slow decline and desperate men bargaining or fighting over whatever scraps they have left. Reviews were split on release, mostly over the violence and the lack of uplift, but the film is now considered a classic of the war genre. 'Johnny Got His Gun' (1971) A Nightmare With No Waking Up Cinemation Industries IMDb: 7.8/10 | Letterboxd: 4.0/5 Johnny Got His Gun traps you inside Joe Bonham, an American soldier who takes an artillery shell in the last days of World War I and comes out of it without arms, legs, or a face. He is deaf, blind, mute, and, to the astonishment of the doctors keeping him alive, conscious. Color memories and fantasies break up a stark black-and-white hospital present, where Joe lies locked inside the horror of his own head. The film is also based on one of the most disturbing books ever written , and Dalton Trumbo adapted his own 1938 novel and directed the picture himself to make sure his anti-war tale of isolation kept the essence of the writing. No war film has ever built a more airtight case against the entire enterprise, and the closing lines are haunting; they will stick with you for a long time. Metallica later cut footage into the "One" video and eventually bought the rights outright, which is how a lot of people my age found the film in the first place. 'The Captain' (2018) What a Uniform Gives You IMDb: 7.3/10 | Letterboxd: 3.7/5 The Captain follows Willi Herold, a 19-year-old Wehrmacht private hunted through the countryside by his own side for desertion in April 1945. He finds an officer's uniform in an abandoned staff car and puts it on to stay warm. Mistaken for a commissioned officer, he sinks into fascist fantasies as he talks his way into command of a camp that executes deserters. Based on a true story . Robert Schwentke's crisp black-and-white feature opens on a strangely comic note, and that tone holds as a scared kid bluffs his way out of one tight spot after another; you almost want to cheer him on. Those early laughs turn out to be the trap, because Herold grows into the rank he stole, and before long he is presiding over executions and savoring every ounce of authority that comes with it . With so much else here leaning relentlessly bleak, this is easily the lightest watch on the list, and a thought-provoking one on how quickly ordinary people fall in line. 'The Painted Bird' (2019) Unending Suffering Bioscop IMDb: 7.3/10 | Letterboxd: 3.6/5 The Painted Bird follows an unnamed Jewish boy across the Eastern European countryside during World War II, passed between the households of strangers after his aunt dies. Václav Marhoul spent eleven years getting the Jerzy Kosinski novel to screen, shot in 35mm black-and-white and using an invented Interslavic dialect, so no single nation could be blamed. The film runs nearly three hours and is broken into chapters named after the people the boy encounters along the way. The walkouts at the Venice premiere are part of the film's reputation, and I can understand why people were rattled by the content. There is an abundance of uncomfortable imagery to contend with, from the abuse of the young boy as he wanders between broken homes, to shocking moments of violence toward others and animals. Whether this is a masterpiece or an endurance test is a fair argument to have, but there is no denying this is one of the most disturbing war movies of the 21st century. https://www.politico.eu/article/keir-sta.text: LONDON — The by-election to replace Keir Starmer as a member of parliament is expected to take place on Oct. 8, two Labour Party officials told POLITICO. Voters in the central London constituency of Holborn and St Pancras will go to the polls next month to elect the ex-PM’s successor in what is likely to be a tense fight between the ruling Labour Party and insurgent Greens. On Monday, Labour moved a writ — the parliamentary procedure to trigger a by-election when a seat becomes vacant — and the two Labour Party officials quoted above, granted anonymity to discuss internal discussions, said it will pave the way for the Oct. 8 date. Advertisement Advertisement The former prime minister stood down from the House of Commons last week. He said he wants to devote more time to international affairs, despite previously pledging to remain an MP until the next general election. In 2024, Starmer held the seat with a 11,572 majority, but faced a strong challenge from a left-wing independent candidate and the Greens. Green Leader Leader Zack Polanski has put himself forward for the party’s nomination, arguing that under him “voters will have someone who will always fight their corner.” He is facing a challenge from Hamza Chowdhury, a councilor in the Camden Green ward, who said the constituency doesn’t need an MP who “makes a few promises and disappears once the votes are counted.” The party’s candidate will be announced on Sept. 11. The election is due to take place less than a week after the Green Party’s annual conference, which takes place in Brighton between Oct. 2 and Oct. 4. Labour’s annual conference takes place in Liverpool from Sept. 27 to Sept. 30. Labour will choose its candidate on Wednesday. Advertisement Advertisement
